Adolphe Sax wished to create a new instrument that would combine the best of both worlds, and thus the first saxophone came into being. According to the passage, which of the following pairs of features characterizes the saxophone that Sax created?
choices: The intensity of its tone is greater than that of the woodwinds, and the variety of its tones is richer than that of the brass
The intensity of its tone is greater than that of the brass, and the variety of its tones is similar to theirs
The intensity of its tone is similar to that of the woodwinds, and the variety of its tones is richer than theirs
The intensity of its tone is similar to that of the woodwinds, and the variety of its tones is richer than that of the brass
explanation: "The best of both worlds" means each strength taken from the family that has it — intensity beyond the woodwinds, variety beyond the brass. (2) exceeds the brass in their own strength; (3) and (4) leave the intensity at the woodwinds' weak level.

steps.stem: In the eighteenth century physiognomy — the doctrine that a person's character can be deduced from his appearance — was regarded as an obvious truth. Today physiognomy is denounced as a pseudo-science, although in recent years it has enjoyed a revival in certain circles that seek to promote a "new physiognomy," a doctrine whose hypotheses are more moderate than those of its predecessor, but which is no less problematic. What can be inferred about the author's opinion of physiognomy?
choices: Physiognomy, which until recently was regarded as a genuine science, is now regarded as problematic because its hypotheses became more moderate upon its revival
The "new physiognomy" is not a pseudo-science, since its hypotheses are more moderate than those of eighteenth-century physiognomy
The moderate hypotheses of the "new physiognomy," unlike those of eighteenth-century physiognomy, have re-established it as a science
Although the attempt to revive physiognomy has succeeded in certain circles, the doctrine is no less problematic and no less a pseudo-science than before
explanation: "No less problematic" is the author's verdict; (2) and (3) treat moderation as rehabilitation, and (1) confuses the cause of the verdict with its timing.

steps.stem: In the seventeenth century the French linguist Claude Bachet, who was also an amateur mathematician, published a book of riddles together with their solutions. One of the riddles asked: what is the smallest number of weights with which any whole number of kilograms from one to forty can be weighed on a balance? Bachet showed that the number is four. Which of the following statements about the riddle is NOT made in the passage?
choices: The riddle concerns not only mathematics but also linguistics
The solution of the riddle is four
The riddle appears in a book of riddles published in the seventeenth century
The solution of the riddle appears in a book published by Claude Bachet
explanation: Bachet's profession is stated; the riddle's subject is arithmetic alone. (2), (3) and (4) are each in the text.

steps.stem: One of the projects in which the American space agency is engaged is the search for life on other planets. Recently, scientists working on the project have taken an interest in "ice cauldrons" — cracks in ice that form distinctive spiral shapes, which can be recognized easily even from very great distances. Ice cauldrons are common near the Earth's north pole, where they are formed by the eruption of volcanoes buried under a layer of ice and snow, and tests carried out on Earth show that such eruptions create an environment that combines heat, moisture and a wide range of minerals. A combination of three of the following claims could explain the scientists' interest in ice cauldrons. Which is the remaining claim?
choices: Since the conditions that form ice cauldrons are not unique to Earth, it is possible that cauldrons are formed on other planets too
The combination of heat, moisture and a wide range of minerals is regarded as an ideal condition for the emergence of life
Spiral-shaped cracks in ice may be formed not only by a volcanic eruption but by other causes as well
The agency has almost no means of searching for life on other planets other than photographing their surfaces from great distances
explanation: (1), (2) and (4) chain into the interest — cauldrons elsewhere, life-friendly conditions, visible from afar; (3) weakens the chain by making the spirals ambiguous.

steps.stem: Political movements tend to create myths about the past in order to shape the future, especially in times of crisis. Thus, at the beginning of the twentieth century, when Socialist Zionism was growing slowly and with great difficulty, it glorified the Bilu movement of the previous generation in an attempt to attach itself to historical roots and so to strengthen its own spiritual foundations. By contrast, the Jewish labor movement in the United States was at that time developing rapidly and its activity was in full swing; it therefore had no need to be nostalgic about the Am Olam movement, its own predecessor. The passage above was written in answer to a question. Which of the following is most likely to be that question?
choices: Why did the difficulties experienced by Socialist Zionism lead it to rely on myths, whereas the success of the Jewish labor movement in the United States did not?
What significance did the myths of Bilu and Am Olam have for the Socialist Zionists on the one hand and for the Jewish labor movement in the United States on the other?
What might explain the fact that the Socialist Zionists found a source of inspiration in the Bilu movement in particular, and not in Am Olam?
Why did the myth of Bilu take root among the Socialist Zionists, whereas Am Olam did not fulfill a similar function for the Jewish labor movement in the United States?
explanation: The passage explains one movement's myth-making and the other's absence of it; (1) presupposes the answer in its wording, (2) asks about significance rather than cause, (3) asks about a choice between the two myths that the passage never compares.

steps.stem: The journalist Jacob Burak wrote: "When people are exposed to an advertisement they assume that it is not the whole truth. The rules of the game are clear to everyone, and people have learned to treat the promises made in advertisements with caution. And so I ask: when will people finally learn to be equally cautious when they read reports of scientific breakthroughs in the popular media?" Which of the following claims is implied by the text?
choices: People should treat advertisements with more caution than they treat reports of scientific breakthroughs in the popular media
People place too much trust in reports of scientific breakthroughs in the popular media
In the past, advertisements were more truthful than they are today
People today are more suspicious of reports of scientific breakthroughs in the popular media than they are of advertisements
explanation: "When will people learn to be equally cautious" presupposes they are not yet cautious enough; (4) reverses it, (1) misplaces the comparison, (3) is unmentioned.

steps.stem: The signature of the celebrated painter Rembrandt appears on many paintings that were done by his pupils. This should not be regarded as forgery, however. In his day the regulations of the painters' guild forbade pupils to sign their own works as long as they were employed in their master's studio; only the master was permitted to sign them. Moreover, the master often corrected his pupils' paintings so as to make them worthy of his signature. A painter's signature thus served to certify the quality of a work. Which of the following is inferred from the text?
choices: Rembrandt signed his pupils' paintings only if he had corrected them
In Rembrandt's day a painter's signature on a painting was not proof that he had painted it himself
Rembrandt's pupils asked him to sign their works, although this was against the guild's regulations
Pupils in Rembrandt's studio signed their own paintings only when Rembrandt declined to sign them
explanation: A signature certified quality, not authorship. (1) turns "often" into "only if"; (3) and (4) contradict the regulation.

steps.stem: The freeing of slaves in Rome was a gradual process, and the first to benefit from it were those slaves whose professional skills in certain trades were superior to those of their masters. From this we learn that the slaves who came from Greece and from other parts of the East — merchants and craftsmen — were freed before the Cimbri, the Teutons and the Lusitanians, who worked mainly in agriculture. According to the passage, why did the Cimbrian, Teutonic and Lusitanian slaves have to wait longer to be freed?
choices: Because they were unskilled at agricultural work
Because the Romans needed their highly developed agricultural skills
Because they worked in a sector in which they did not have the advantage of superior skill
Because they had not come to Rome from the East
explanation: The criterion is superior skill relative to the masters, and Roman masters knew agriculture; (1), (2) and (4) supply facts the passage does not give.

steps.stem: In photographs taken from the moon's surface the sky above the moon looks dark, yet in many of them no stars are visible. Puzzling as this is, there is an explanation. The photographs that show a dark sky without stars are not photographs of the night sky but of the day sky. On Earth the day sky looks blue because of the way the atmosphere scatters sunlight; the moon has no atmosphere, and so its sky is dark by day as well. But because the moon's surface is very light in color, when sunlight strikes it by day the area above the surface is lit so brightly that the faint light of the stars is hard to make out. Which of the following claims follows from the passage?
choices: If the moon had an atmosphere, it would not be possible to see stars in its sky even at night
The atmosphere surrounding the Earth is what enables us to see stars in its night sky
It is harder to see stars in the moon's night sky than in the Earth's night sky
If the moon's surface were darker, it would be easier to see stars in its sky by day
explanation: The brightness of the lit surface is what hides the stars; a darker surface would hide them less. (1), (2) and (3) are not supported.

steps.stem: Discussing the vision of the modern city that the architect Le Corbusier presented in 1922, the urban planner Jane Jacobs wrote: "His city is like a wonderful mechanical toy, and its design — as a work of architecture — is simple and harmonious, highly organized and highly clear." Yet with regard to the actual functioning of a city, she claims, his plan "tells nothing but lies": it offers no answer to the problems of managing life in a city, and is no more than an imaginary vision drawn up by someone who does not understand how real cities work. Which of the following best presents Jacobs's opinion of Le Corbusier's plan?
choices: The impressive features of the city he planned outweigh its shortcomings
His plan was impressive as architecture, but a city built according to it would not function properly
At first sight his plan appeared organized and clear, but in practice it was not so at all
Since he did not understand how real cities work, his design was not sufficiently organized and clear
explanation: The praise is for the design as architecture and the blame for its working as a city; (3) and (4) turn the praise into an illusion, (1) weighs the two the wrong way.

steps.stem: The following two paragraphs are excerpts from a book that analyzes disagreements and discussions: a. "In most cases a disagreement turns on a single main idea. But our view of the world is built like a network — each idea is bound up with a vast number of others — and the network does not allow any single idea to change drastically." b. "Each side in a discussion expects the other to be open to its arguments; but at the same time each side is afraid to admit a mistake, which would be taken as a sign of weakness. Thus discussions often turn into contests whose chief aim is not to be beaten." Which of the following is the question the two excerpts together answer?
choices: How to prevent the sides in a discussion from entrenching themselves in their positions, and to enable them to reach agreement
Why it is important to be open to the arguments of the other side in a discussion
How the way we connect ideas to one another affects our ability to hold productive discussions
Why disagreements and discussions only rarely end with one side being persuaded by the other
explanation: Both excerpts give reasons persuasion fails — one cognitive, one social. (1) and (2) are prescriptions the excerpts do not offer; (3) fits only the first.

steps.stem: At the beginning of the modern era the idea that the human body is like a machine was widespread in the West, and it shaped the development of medicine as well. Just as we tend not to interfere with a machine while it is working properly, so physicians and researchers took no interest in the healthy body, and examined the body chiefly when something in it had ceased to function or had "broken down." Thus medicine in fact developed out of the study of the sick. According to the passage, medicine developed out of the study of the sick —
choices: because physicians and researchers learned about the healthy body from observing machines, and only disease compelled them to examine an actual body
because physicians assumed that just as machines tend to break down, so the human body cannot always be healthy
because comparing the human body to a machine was a mistake that caused many failures in attempts to heal the body
because, like a machine, the body drew attention only when it stopped working properly
explanation: The analogy is about when one looks, not about where knowledge comes from; (1) misreads the source of knowledge, (2) invents an assumption, (3) invents a verdict.

steps.stem: The research of Frans de Waal shows that bonobo apes display moral behavior — a finding that challenges the human sense of superiority. It makes life difficult for those who would draw a sharp line between human beings and all other living creatures, but the message of the research is an optimistic one: if human morality has roots in the very distant past, we may expect it to be more resilient in the face of cultural and historical change. Which of the following is NOT implied by the text?
choices: The fact that bonobos display moral behavior is proof that human morality already existed in humankind's ancient past
If the origin of morality does not lie in humankind's ancient past, morality may be more vulnerable to cultural and historical influences
Some of those who would draw a sharp line between human beings and other creatures have held that no other creature displays moral behavior
Although there appears to be no clear dividing line between human beings and other creatures with regard to morality, human morality may prove more durable than had been thought
explanation: The text says "if human morality has roots in the distant past" — a condition, not a proof; (2), (3) and (4) each follow from the text's claims.

steps.stem: The myth of the "normal family" persists despite the sociological and anthropological studies of the family in modern times, and this is due in large part to television series. The harmonious image these series commonly present — of people who meet life's trials without anger and always cooperate with one another — shatters the moment one observes a real family facing its daily problems. It is therefore worrying that therapists often assess the functioning of the families they treat by comparing them with this idealized image. Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
choices: The task of family therapists is to help the members of a family improve their daily functioning and their ability to cope with problems
It is true that the characters seen on television create an image that is not wholly accurate, but the therapists' tendency to rely on it is understandable
Many therapists are influenced by the image of the family created by sociological and anthropological studies
The standard by which therapists often assess the functioning of the families they treat is unfair, because it is unrealistic
explanation: The passage builds to the worry about the therapists' standard; (2) excuses what it condemns, (3) names the wrong source of the image, (1) describes a task the passage does not discuss.

steps.stem: In 1923 the astronomer Edwin Hubble discovered a Cepheid star in the spiral nebula Andromeda. A few years earlier astronomers had worked out how to calculate the distance between a star of this kind and the Earth, and the discovery therefore enabled Hubble to estimate, for the first time, the distance of Andromeda from the Earth: about nine hundred thousand light-years — far greater than the diameter of the Milky Way, the galaxy in which the Earth lies. In this way it came to be recognized that Andromeda is not part of the Milky Way but a separate galaxy, and hence that the Milky Way is not the only galaxy in the universe. According to the passage, what was the part played by Hubble's discovery?
choices: It made it possible to apply existing knowledge to calculate the distance of Andromeda, and so to show that Andromeda lies outside the Milky Way
It showed that Cepheid stars, which are found in Andromeda, are not found in the Milky Way
It pointed to a new way of calculating the distances of stars from the Earth, and so made it possible to show the size of the Milky Way
It showed that spiral nebulae are in fact galaxies, and hence it can be inferred that Andromeda, being a spiral nebula, is a galaxy
explanation: The method already existed; the discovery supplied the star to apply it to. (3) credits Hubble with the method; (2) and (4) reverse the direction of the inference.

steps.stem: The following appeared in a medical journal: "Unlike the other medications for this disease, the new medication does not attack the concentration of X-type bacteria in the throat — the bacteria that cause the disease — and therefore it does not bring about recovery. It is becoming clear, however, that the medication is necessary for long-term treatment, because it attacks the X bacteria that spread from the throat into the bloodstream while the patient was ill. These bacteria remain in the bloodstream even after recovery, and it has recently been found that they are what cause the disease to recur." Which of the following is implied by the passage?
choices: The new medication is unique in preventing X bacteria from passing from the throat into the bloodstream
The medications that attack the X bacteria concentrated in the throat do not prevent the disease from recurring once the patient has recovered
The new medication can help only patients in whom the disease has already recurred several times
The fact that the new medication prevents recurrence makes the existing medications unnecessary
explanation: The existing medications act in the throat, and recurrence comes from the bloodstream. (1) confuses attacking with preventing passage; (3) and (4) go beyond the text.

steps.stem: Since the 1950s there have been two main approaches to the study of the language of the writer Haim Hazaz. The first regards the linguistic abundance characteristic of his works as a matter of function — a means of representing the fictional reality faithfully and realistically. According to the second, his language has, besides its basic role as a descriptive instrument, a purpose of its own: it demands that readers immerse themselves in its inherent aesthetics, which are neither bound by nor conditional on the reality it describes. Which of the following questions do the two approaches dispute?
choices: Are the aesthetics of Hazaz's style bound by the fictional reality of his works, or do they create it?
Does Hazaz's style contribute to the creation of the fictional world of his works, or only to their aesthetics?
Is Hazaz's style one of the strong points of his works or one of their weak points?
Does Hazaz's style have a purpose beyond shaping the world he creates in his works?
explanation: Both approaches grant the descriptive role; they differ over whether there is anything more. (2) denies the shared ground; (1) and (3) are not the issue.

steps.stem: In a lecture on the study of the universe the lecturer said: "Everyone knows that when many fish swim in a small aquarium the crowding in it is great, but that if the aquarium is enlarged the crowding lessens. According to one theory, shortly after the universe came into being its volume grew, yet the density of the matter in it remained as it had been; hence, necessarily, the quantity of matter in it grew as well. In the terms of the aquarium example we would say, then, that ____." Which of the following best completes the lecturer's words?
choices: the number of fish in the aquarium rose, while the size of the aquarium remained as it was
when the aquarium was enlarged the crowding in it did not change, since the number of fish in it remained as it was
when the aquarium was enlarged, the number of fish in it grew as well
the number of fish in the aquarium ceased to affect the crowding in it
explanation: Volume up and density unchanged means quantity up — more fish in a bigger tank. (1) keeps the tank the same size; (2) keeps the fish the same and so would lower the crowding; (4) breaks the relation the example rests on.

steps.stem: Zoologists observing a group of chimpanzees noticed that when the group meets an unfamiliar object — a mirror, say, or a length of rope — the young of the group are the first to approach it, while the adults keep their distance; that the adults approach only after the young have handled the object for some time without harm; and that the order in which the adults then approach follows their rank in the group, the leader last of all. For which of the following questions does the passage NOT provide an answer?
choices: Which members of the group are the first to approach an unfamiliar object?
When do the adults approach an unfamiliar object?
Why do the young approach an unfamiliar object before the adults?
In what order do the adults approach an unfamiliar object?
explanation: The passage describes the sequence in detail but never gives the young's reason; (1), (2) and (4) are each answered directly.

steps.stem: Moshe: "Most of my friends who were studying history have stopped and gone over to economics." Chaim: "That is further proof that people prefer to invest less in enriching their inner world and more in studies that will let them find work easily." From Chaim's words it follows that in his view, unlike the study of history, the study of economics ____ finding work easily, ____ enriching a person's inner world.
choices: does not help / but contributes to
makes possible / but contributes far less to
helps / but at the price of renouncing altogether
does indeed make possible / but contributes much to
explanation: Chaim's remark pairs economics with work and history with the inner world, as a matter of more and less. (1) reverses the first half; (3) makes the second half absolute; (4) removes the contrast.

steps.stem: Architecture has always been a faithful reflection of social, economic and cultural conceptions. So it is with Israeli architecture, which reflects, among other things, the tension characteristic of countries of immigration — between the foreign and the native, between the import of ideas and approaches from abroad and the attempt to draw on what is local. Which of the following claims is made in the passage?
choices: The uniqueness of Israeli architecture lies in its faithful reflection of social, economic and cultural conceptions
Unlike the architecture of other countries of immigration, Israeli architecture rests not only on imports but also on local traditions
Like architecture in general, Israeli architecture reflects social, economic and cultural conceptions
The central subject around which Israeli architecture took shape is the tension characteristic of countries of immigration
explanation: (1) makes unique what the passage says is universal; (2) invents a contrast with other countries; (4) promotes "among other things" to "the central subject."

steps.stem: In an article on Dante's treatise "Monarchy" it was written: "On the face of it, Dante's political treatise does not reach the intellectual height of his poetry; but it is not proper to hold, on the strength of a work written six hundred and fifty years ago, that Dante's ideas are not relevant to our own time, and we cannot be sure of it without close study. And as in poetry, so in political thought — Dante's ideas were ahead of his time by several centuries." Which of the following claims is made in the passage?
choices: The intellectual level of Dante's political treatise cannot be properly assessed without studying it in depth
We shall never know whether Dante's poetry was ahead of its time
If readers examine Dante's political treatise with an understanding of the ideas of his period, it turns out to be of higher value than his poetry
Because of the distance in time, a proper assessment of Dante's political treatise requires an investment of study and reflection
explanation: "We cannot be sure without close study" of a work "written six hundred and fifty years ago" — the distance is the reason. (1) drops the reason; (2) contradicts the last sentence; (3) reverses the comparison with the poetry.

steps.stem: The cycle of poems "Empty Dances" by the poet Hezi Laskly stands in a state of constant "inner contradiction." Laskly sets out to write, in effect, the weaknesses of language: he displays the problems of using words and presents language as an empty instrument that cannot convey the shades of thought or feeling. Yet at the same time he presents his poetry, which lays bare the dance, as the only language that makes self-expression and genuine communication possible. Which of the following best fits the "inner contradiction" described in the passage?
choices: Laskly tries to express himself by means of non-verbal instruments, such as the dance
Laskly called his cycle "Empty Dances," though its claim is that verbal language is empty
Laskly seeks to describe abstract things, such as thoughts or feelings, by means of something concrete, such as verbal language
Laskly tries to use words to describe the helplessness of verbal language
explanation: The contradiction is between the medium and the message about it. (1) contradicts "his poetry"; (2) and (3) locate the contradiction where the passage does not.

steps.stem: The French writer Albert Camus said: "As a remedy for life in society I propose the great city. In our day it is the only desert left to us." Which of the following claims does NOT arise from Camus's words?
choices: Life in society is a kind of illness
Life in the great city is a life of solitude
In our day it is hard for a person to be alone
Life in the great city is expensive
explanation: A remedy implies an illness, a desert implies solitude, "the only desert left" implies its scarcity; cost is nowhere in the words.

steps.stem: In a book on globalization it was written: "Globalization is remarkable in that it unites and in that it divides. Alongside the strengthening of the worldwide flow of business, money and information, a separation between populations is being fixed and a barrier raised between those who enjoy the fruits of globalization and those who do not. The mobility that globalization makes possible — social as well as physical — becomes an object of desire, but it is a prized resource that is distributed unequally." Which of the following claims best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Although globalization seeks to benefit everyone equally, it fails, since not all populations enjoy equal mobility
Since the advantage of globalization is the worldwide flow of information, and since it harms the mobility of certain populations, there are populations that globalization harms
Although the worldwide flow of business, money and information has an effect on everyone, it raises a barrier between populations that enjoy great mobility and populations that do not
The harm done to the mobility of certain populations is what prevents the worldwide flow of business, money and information
explanation: (1) attributes an aim; (2) makes the flow itself the harm; (4) reverses cause and effect.

steps.stem: In his book on the openings of stories, Amos Oz wrote: "The title of Chekhov's story 'Rothschild's Fiddle' leads the reader astray in four ways: the Rothschild of the story is not the famous banker, he is not the narrator, the fiddle is not his until the last pages, and he is not the story's hero but only a secondary figure, a poor and wretched clerk." From the passage it emerges that Oz makes three of the following four assumptions. Which is the remaining one?
choices: When the title of a story mentions a name, the reader assumes it is the name of the story's hero
The name Rothschild is identified with the famous banker
From the expression "X's fiddle" one infers that the fiddle belongs to X
The main figures in stories are usually not poor and wretched people
explanation: Each of the first three assumptions is needed for one of the "ways" the title misleads; the fourth concerns what happens inside the story, not what the title leads a reader to expect.

steps.stem: In an article it was written: "All empires decline in the end — an empire lasts about three hundred years on average. Look at Rome: its prosperity drew migrants to it; the new population brought with it new values and customs that undermined the empire's strength, and they brought it down from within. In the United States, which can be regarded as an empire about a hundred and fifty years old, a similar process is to be expected before long." According to the passage, which of the following is NOT expected to happen in the United States?
choices: It will continue to flourish as an empire for another three hundred years
A new population will arrive in it
The values prevailing in it will change
Internal processes will bring about its collapse
explanation: At a hundred and fifty years, another three hundred would break the average the passage asserts; (2), (3) and (4) are the stages of the Roman pattern the passage predicts.

steps.stem: Leah Goldberg gave her opinion on the literary and theoretical problems involved in writing literature for children, and from time to time set out her views on them. She never formulated a "theory of children's literature" in a central, comprehensive essay; but her thinking on these problems was not devoid of systematic order and conceptual consistency. Which of the following sentences best summarizes what is said in the passage?
choices: Although Leah Goldberg wrote a great deal about the problems of writing for children, she did not write a comprehensive essay defining a "theory of children's literature," because she believed that writing such an essay would raise literary and theoretical problems

Although Leah Goldberg dealt regularly with the problems of writing for children, and at times set out her opinion on them, she did not put the things down in writing, since her positions were not systematic

Leah Goldberg held an orderly and consistent conception of children's literature, which she expressed on several occasions, although she never wrote a comprehensive essay presenting her positions on the subject
Leah Goldberg was aware of the literary and theoretical problems of writing for children, but they did not deter her from engaging in such writing herself
explanation: "Not devoid of order and consistency" affirms the order; (2) denies it, (1) supplies a motive, (4) changes the subject to her own writing for children.

steps.stem: The branches of the river Pregel divide the city of Königsberg into four parts, and between the four parts stretch seven bridges. For years the city's inhabitants tried to find a route that would cross each of the seven bridges exactly once, without crossing any bridge twice, and they did not succeed. In 1735 the mathematician Leonhard Euler proved that such a route is impossible. In the article he published following this discovery he named it "the Königsberg bridge problem," and showed that it exists in many situations, theoretical and practical alike. In doing so he laid the foundations of graph theory — a central field of mathematics. Which of the following claims arises from the passage?
choices: In 1735 graph theory was a new field of mathematics, known to few
No one ever succeeded in crossing all the bridges of Königsberg without crossing one of them twice
Euler was the first to show that all the bridges can be crossed if one of them is crossed twice
In his article Euler showed that other cities divided by rivers have the same bridge problem
explanation: What is impossible was never done. (1) puts the field before its founding; (3) and (4) are not in the passage.

steps.stem: Stars, such as the sun, are heavenly bodies that emit radiation; around some of them orbit planets, such as the Earth, which emit no radiation. Scientists estimate that around every star in our galaxy orbit, on average, about 1.6 planets, but they note that this estimate is low. The method of estimation rests on observing stars, most of them far from the Earth: when planets orbit a star they pass between it and the Earth and cause changes in the star's brightness. But such changes can be detected only when the planets are far from the star they orbit and not too small in relation to it. According to the passage, why does the method yield an underestimate?
choices: Because small planets orbiting a star, or planets close to it, do not change the star's brightness enough for the change to be detected
Because it is reasonable to suppose that besides the stars we can identify there are stars hard to identify, and planets orbit them too
Because it is reasonable to suppose that there are also planets small in relation to their star, both far from it and near it, which are only a small fraction of all planets
Because it rests on observing stars far from the Earth and on changes in their brightness, and is not suited to detecting planets near the Earth
explanation: Planets the method cannot see are planets the count misses. (2) and (4) concern the stars, not the planets; (3) makes the missed planets few.

steps.stem: The wings of the cicada — a kind of winged insect — are covered with a sort of microscopic spikes, and when a bacterium tries to settle on them its membrane is stretched between the spikes and torn. Researchers hope to develop in the future an artificial material of similar structure and to coat with it the surfaces on which bacteria settle and from which they pass to human beings — door handles, taps and elevator buttons, for instance. Which of the following claims is correct according to the passage?
choices: The researchers hope to develop artificial surfaces that can be coated with material taken from cicada wings
Thanks to the structure of their wings, cicadas are not harmed by the bacteria that settle on them
Bacteria tend to settle on surfaces covered with microscopic spikes
The microscopic structure of door handles, taps and elevator buttons resembles that of cicada wings
explanation: Bacteria that are torn on landing cannot harm the insect. (1) confuses an artificial imitation with the natural material; (3) reverses the effect; (4) describes the surfaces as they are hoped to become.

steps.stem: According to Aristotle, dialectic and rhetoric are both arts of the use of language. The aim of dialectic is to reach the truth, and it is therefore indifferent to who the speaker and the hearer are — for truth does not depend on the situation in which it is stated. The aim of rhetoric, by contrast, is to persuade, and persuasion is by its nature an activity between persons, bound up with a system of relations between a particular speaker and particular hearers. Which of the following sentences best summarizes the difference between dialectic and rhetoric according to Aristotle?
choices: Rhetoric is an instrument that serves a particular speaker to persuade a particular hearer, whereas dialectic requires the absence of speaker and hearer in order to reach the truth
Although both are arts of the use of language, dialectic is indifferent to the situation, whereas rhetoric is indifferent to the truth
The relation between speaker and hearer is relevant only to rhetoric, whose aim is to persuade, and not to dialectic, whose aim is to reach the truth
The identity of the speaker and the hearer matters only in rhetoric, since it, unlike dialectic, aims at reaching the truth in a particular situation
explanation: (1) turns indifference into absence; (2) attributes to rhetoric an indifference the passage does not; (4) gives rhetoric the aim of dialectic.

steps.stem: In a television review it was written: "As one who knows the series 'All Honor to Sher,' I too received with enthusiasm the announcement of a special episode marking half a century since the last episode was broadcast. But when it emerged that the special episode is nothing more than a filmed theatrical staging of several of the original episodes, my enthusiasm turned to disappointment: I knew at once that the polished acting, so vital on the stage, would look exaggerated on the small screen." Which of the following does NOT follow from the passage?
choices: In retrospect the critic realized that his joy at the announcement had not been justified
In the critic's view the acting of television actors should be more restrained than that of stage actors
The critic did not enjoy the theatrical staging on which the special episode is based
The plot of the special episode was already familiar to viewers of the series
explanation: The critic predicted how the staging would look on television; nothing says he saw it. (1), (2) and (4) each follow.

steps.stem: The meat industry around the world is responsible for the emission of more greenhouse gases than almost any other source. On the basis of data from the United Nations' food and agriculture organization, the industry's "contribution" is estimated at eighteen percent of the world's emissions of greenhouse gases; in the scale of pollution it is thus second only to power stations. Which of the following claims is correct according to the passage?
choices: Even power stations pollute less than the meat industry
Apart from power stations, no source is responsible for more greenhouse-gas emissions than the meat industry
In the past the meat industry was the most polluting source, but today it is responsible for only eighteen percent of emissions
The meat industry is responsible for eighteen percent of emissions, and power stations for the rest
explanation: "Second only to power stations" gives (2) and denies (1); (3) invents a past; (4) turns the rest of the emissions into one source.

steps.stem: According to Jean-Paul Sartre, a human being is free without limit. One who makes his freedom depend on external factors — social norms, an ideology, or any other anchor — is fleeing from himself, and thereby fails to realize his freedom in any of his decisions; whoever acts so is not an authentic person. According to Sartre, who is an authentic person?
choices: A person whose freedom is without limit
A person who realizes his freedom in his decisions
A person with a clear ideology and a developed sense of belonging
A person who acts openly against social norms
explanation: Freedom without limit is everyone's; authenticity is realizing it. (3) is Sartre's example of flight; (4) confuses defiance of norms with independence of them.

steps.stem: At the end of the eighteenth century, with the rise of the liberal regime in the United States, the use of pen names in American journalism faded. There is irony in this: the conservative discourse that had prevailed before, with its banner of communal values, was more comfortable for writers who wished to guard their privacy and to hide behind an invented identity than the liberal democracy which, although it raised the individual and the value of privacy on high, could not tolerate an offense against the value of transparency. What is the irony the passage describes?
choices: It was the conservative discourse, concerned with the public and not with the private, that shaped the norms of privacy protection for writers in the first years of liberal democracy
The conservative discourse, which set the community at the center, allowed writers a privacy that was no longer possible under the new regime, which supposedly sanctified the individual
The fading of pen names, which allow a writer to hide behind an invented identity, hints at the liberal regime's preference for the private over the public
Hiding behind an invented identity, which allowed writers to guard their privacy, was consistent with the conservative communal ideology
explanation: The irony is the mismatch between a regime's values and their effect. (4) is the half without the mismatch; (1) and (3) invent claims.

steps.stem: In an experiment, participants watched another person being deceived, and were then asked to tell the deceived person about it. While they watched the deception a rise in their heart rate was recorded, but as soon as they had passed the information to the deceived person their heart rate returned to normal. On the basis of these findings and a number of assumptions, the researchers concluded that an attempt to right a social wrong can have a positive effect on health. Three of the following assumptions are among those the researchers relied on. Which is the remaining one?
choices: Telling a person that he has been deceived is an attempt to right a social wrong
The return of the heart rate to normal is a positive effect on health
When a person watches another being deceived, his heart rate rises
Telling the deceived person is what caused the participants' heart rate to return to normal
explanation: That is a finding of the experiment, not an assumption; the other three are the bridges from the findings to the conclusion.

steps.stem: In his ruling the judge wrote: "I am prepared to assume that the employer did not intend to harm the employee's advancement when he fixed her salary. But the employer's intention is not relevant to the matter before us, since the test of whether there was discrimination is objective and not subjective. To determine whether there was discrimination one must examine the final result as it appears in reality." Which of the following claims arises from the ruling?
choices: Even if an employee feels discriminated against, one must examine whether the objective data show that the employer intended to discriminate
It is enough to examine the employee's situation against that of other employees in order to determine whether there was discrimination, even if there was no intention to discriminate
An employee's advancement may be blocked even when there is no evidence that the employer discriminated against her
Even if there is no evidence that an employee was intentionally discriminated against, discrimination may be found in her situation if the employer intended to discriminate
explanation: Intention is irrelevant and result is decisive. (1) and (4) restore intention to the test; (3) is not what the ruling says.

steps.stem: One of the Islamic orders of the Middle Ages was the Naqshbandiyya. The order was distinguished by "seclusion within society": a person is able to feel God within himself and to concentrate on Him while remaining involved in the affairs of the world. This conception ruled out withdrawal from worldly affairs and created a framework in which political activity is legitimate from the spiritual point of view. Even material possessions are legitimate, and indeed symbolize God's grace, so long as the person is detached from them in spirit and their presence and their absence are alike to him. Which of the following sentences best summarizes the order's distinctive conception?
choices: A person should concentrate on the worship of God and detach himself from material possessions and political activity
A person must not withdraw from the affairs of the world, since he could not then hold possessions or engage in politics
A person should be detached in spirit from the affairs of the world and feel God within himself, but without withdrawing from society
A person cannot engage in politics or seek possessions unless he feels God within himself
explanation: (1) is the withdrawal the order rejected; (2) makes possessions the reason for staying; (4) turns a permission into a precondition.

steps.stem: In recent years astronomical research has shown that order and law can be found in the universe only if the universe is taken into account as a whole, and if every component of it — from small asteroids through stars and clusters of stars to galaxies — is regarded as developing and changing all the time. What arises from the passage?
choices: Astronomers have recently shown that one cannot argue that the universe changes all the time without assuming order and law in it
Astronomers have recently discovered that the universe changes all the time, and from this discovery they learned which laws operate in it
From the assumption that the universe changes all the time, astronomers arrived at the conclusion that there is order and law in it
Astronomers have recently understood that unless they assume that the universe changes all the time, they will not be able to find order and law in it
explanation: The change is the condition of finding the order; (1) reverses the condition, (2) makes the change a discovery, (3) makes the order a conclusion from it.

steps.stem: Dividing one's attention between two (or more) sources of information is one of the kinds of division that take place in consciousness. Other kinds occur, for instance, when a person takes in information and reacts to it at the same time, or when a person performs an action and at the same time plans his next actions. Which of the following examples does NOT illustrate any of the kinds of division mentioned in the passage?
choices: A person translating a speaker's words for an audience while the speaker is speaking
A person clearing dishes from the table and dropping one of them
A person driving a car and listening to the radio
A person who is about to telephone someone, and while looking for the telephone weighs what he will say
explanation: Dropping a dish is a mishap, not a second task; (1) is take in and react, (3) is two sources, (4) is act and plan.

steps.stem: Absolute pitch is the ability to identify at once the exact pitch of a tone, not by relation to another tone. It is usual to distinguish two kinds of absolute pitch — active and passive. Those who possess active absolute pitch, besides being able to identify tones, are also able to produce by singing any tone that is asked of them. What is claimed in the passage about those who possess absolute pitch?
choices: Those with passive absolute pitch can identify a tone at once but not produce it, whereas those with active absolute pitch can produce a tone but not always identify it
Those with active absolute pitch can sing any tone without relation to another tone, whereas those with passive absolute pitch can do so only by relation to another
Those with active absolute pitch can identify and produce tones more accurately than those with passive absolute pitch
Those of both kinds can identify a tone at once, but only those with active absolute pitch can also sing any tone asked of them
explanation: "Besides being able to identify" keeps identification for both. (1) takes it from the active, (2) gives the passive a relative ability, (3) turns a difference of kind into one of degree.

steps.stem: The scholars Fenstermacher and Soltis identify three main approaches to education: the executive approach, in which the teacher's task is to lead the pupil to high achievement; the therapist approach, in which the teacher's task is to help the pupil reach self-realization; and the liberationist approach, in which the teacher's task is to broaden the pupil's horizons and to teach him new ways of thinking. Neil Postman was never among the supporters of the executive approach: his early writings reflect the therapist approach, and his later writings a position that combines it with the liberationist approach. Which of the following best describes Postman's approach in his later writings?
choices: The teacher should teach the pupil new ways of thinking that will let him broaden his horizons
The teacher should teach the pupil ways of thinking that will help him realize himself and reach high achievement
The teacher should help the pupil reach self-realization, even at the price of lower achievement
The teacher should strive to broaden the pupil's horizons and in that way help him reach self-realization
explanation: A combination of the therapist and the liberationist; (1) is the liberationist alone, (3) the therapist alone, (2) brings in the executive.

steps.stem: Of the German historian Leopold von Ranke (1795–1886) it was written: "Ranke was by nature a moderate man, but at times his moderation caused him to miss an opportune hour that would never return. As a historian, Ranke was able to recognize decisive moments even as they occurred in his own time; but because of his moderate temperament he lacked the daring and the resolve to exploit that ability in order to act and to influence the fate of his homeland." Which of the following sentences best summarizes what was written about Ranke?
choices: As a historian Ranke had the skill to recognize decisive moments in his own time, but because of his moderate nature he did not use it to influence the society in which he lived
Ranke was a moderate man, but his moderation was an obstacle to influencing society, since influence requires daring and resolve, which he lacked
Because of his moderation Ranke did not succeed in recognizing the important moments in which he could have influenced society
Thanks to his skill in recognizing decisive moments Ranke had the power to influence society, but as a moderate man he never tried to do so
explanation: (3) contradicts "was able to recognize"; (2) drops the skill; (4) turns a lack of daring into never trying.

steps.stem: A "black body" is a term of physics for an object that absorbs all the radiation that strikes it and reflects none. Nevertheless, a black body emits radiation of its own, whose intensity depends only on its temperature. According to classical physics, a black body would emit at every moment radiation of unlimited intensity — that is, it would emit infinite energy, which is physically impossible. This contradiction led Max Planck to the insights that became the foundation of quantum theory. Which of the following claims does NOT arise from the passage?
choices: The temperature of a black body does not depend on the radiation it absorbs
Quantum theory grapples with a contradiction that arises from classical physics
Physically, a body cannot emit infinite energy
If a body emits radiation, it emits energy
explanation: The passage speaks of what the emission depends on, not of what the temperature depends on. (2), (3) and (4) are each stated.

steps.stem: Jimmy Carter's entry into the White House in January 1977 brought a dramatic change in American foreign policy. The forcefulness that had characterized it in Nixon's time — and that found conspicuous expression in May 1970 in the opening of a military campaign against North Vietnamese forces deployed on Cambodian territory — gave way to an approach of opposite purpose. The military campaign of May 1970 is presented in the passage as an example of —
choices: the weakness of American foreign policy in Carter's time
the forceful foreign policy of the United States in Nixon's time
the influence of the North Vietnamese forces in Cambodia on American policy
the dramatic change that Carter brought about
explanation: The campaign is the "conspicuous expression" of the earlier forcefulness.

steps.stem: The silver mines of Potosí were depleted, and there was therefore no economic justification for mechanized mining in them. Despite the fall in output, however, profits rose, since the old-fashioned methods of work turned the mines into a tourist attraction. Which of the following claims does NOT follow from the passage?
choices: Had the mines not been depleted, mechanized mining in them would probably have been justified
Had the mines been worked by mechanized methods, they would probably not have become a tourist attraction
Had the mines not become a tourist attraction, profits would probably have fallen
The fall in output is probably what prevented mechanized mining in the mines
explanation: Depletion, not the fall in output, is the reason mechanization was unjustified; the fall in output is a consequence, not a cause. (1), (2) and (3) each reverse one of the passage's links legitimately.

steps.stem: The researcher Otto Warburg argued that cells become cancerous when, instead of receiving their energy from the mitochondria — the energy units of the cell — they pass to obtaining it by the process of glycolysis. As a rule this happens when a cell is short of oxygen; but Warburg found that cancer cells obtain their energy by glycolysis even when they have enough oxygen. Warburg's idea was rejected, among other things because of the argument of the researcher Hans Krebs that Warburg's findings are only a symptom of cancer, and that glycolysis takes place in cancer cells because their mitochondria are defective. What was the dispute between Warburg and Krebs?
choices: Warburg argued that glycolysis takes place in cancer cells because they have much oxygen, whereas Krebs argued that it takes place because their mitochondria are defective
Warburg argued that the conspicuous symptom of cancer cells is obtaining energy by glycolysis, whereas Krebs argued that the conspicuous symptom is their defective mitochondria
Warburg argued that obtaining energy by glycolysis is what causes cancer, whereas Krebs argued that the mitochondria of cancer cells are damaged and that this is why they obtain energy by glycolysis
Warburg argued that glycolysis takes place even when there is enough oxygen, whereas Krebs argued that when there is enough oxygen cells obtain their energy from the mitochondria
explanation: Cause against symptom. (1) misstates Warburg's reason; (2) makes both speak of symptoms; (4) invents a disagreement about oxygen.

steps.stem: The British mathematician Irving Good wrote in 1965: "Let us define an ultra-intelligent machine as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any person, however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultra-intelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then be an 'intelligence explosion,' and the intelligence of man would be left far behind. Thus the first ultra-intelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make." According to what is implied by Good's words, why will man not need to make any invention after the ultra-intelligent machine?
choices: Because the ultra-intelligent machine will exhaust man's inventive capacity, and he will be unable to invent anything better than it
Because if the intelligence of man is left behind, no further machines will be invented for man, but only for the machines themselves
Because the inventive capacity of the machine surpasses that of man, so that it will be able to make any invention better than man could
Because the machine rests on intelligence, and machines surpass man in cleverness, so that there will be no need for inventions that are not machines
explanation: The argument runs through the machine's ability to design; (1) makes it a limit on man, (2) and (4) invent consequences.

steps.stem: Material culture — the objects made by human hands or used by them — is a concern mainly of anthropologists who study pre-literate cultures. Such cultures have no written history, and the anthropologists seize on every find in order to learn from it about the symbols of those cultures and about the way of life that was lived in them. According to what is implied by the passage, why do anthropologists who study later cultures deal little with material culture?
choices: Because they are able to learn about the symbols and the way of life of the cultures they study by means of their written history
Because the information about later cultures that can be obtained from material culture is less than the information about earlier cultures
Because they are not interested in the way of life and the symbols of the cultures they study, but in other features
Because the written history of the cultures they study provides little information about their material culture
explanation: What the pre-literate cultures lack is what the later ones have. (2), (3) and (4) supply reasons the passage does not.

steps.stem: Even after the modern era had begun, much of the spirit of the Middle Ages still remained in Europe, though with the passing of time more and more instances appeared of human power so unlike what had gone before as to astonish. And so the broadening of man's horizons in the modern era advanced hidden from view, in a mysterious way. Which of the following claims best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: The passage from the conceptions of the Middle Ages to those of the modern era was not sharp but gradual
In practice the modern era began earlier than is commonly thought
It is hard to explain why man's horizons broadened in the modern era
New human powers appeared in the Middle Ages and were realized in full only in the modern era
explanation: (2) and (4) shift the dating; (3) mistakes "hidden" for "inexplicable."

steps.stem: Like most inventions, the telephone has many "inventors." They worked on systems for transmitting sound in the second half of the nineteenth century, the period in which the technological principles underlying the telephone were discovered. The invention is generally attributed to Alexander Graham Bell, who registered a patent on the device in 1876; but in Italy Antonio Meucci is regarded as the inventor of the telephone, and in Germany Philipp Reis. Which of the following claims is correct according to the passage?
choices: Reis invented the telephone in Germany, and Bell spread the invention around the world
Bell registered the patent on the telephone, but Reis is its true inventor
Both Bell and Reis are credited with the invention of the telephone, but Bell is the one who registered the patent
Bell discovered the principles of the telephone, and Reis built the device
explanation: The passage attributes, it does not adjudicate; (2) and (4) decide what it leaves open, (1) invents a role for Bell.

steps.stem: In reply to a question she was asked, Professor Brightman said: "Many animals can recognize themselves in a mirror; rats make sounds resembling laughter when they are tickled; parrots and dogs show signs of distress when those close to them die. These phenomena confirm what is already known: animals have a soul and an emotional world. And is it not logical that where there is a soul, diseases of the soul can develop as well?" Which of the following questions is most likely to be the one Professor Brightman was answering?
choices: What evidence is there that animals have an emotional life?
Which species of animals have a soul?
Do animals have a soul and an emotional world?
Do diseases of the soul exist in animals as well?
explanation: She treats the soul as known and argues toward the diseases; (1) and (3) are the premises, not the question.

steps.stem: "Invasive species" are animals or plants that were brought to a new place, outside their natural range, and that spread there rapidly and establish themselves. At times local species too spread rapidly, but these are defined as "proliferating species." The distinction between the two is important for the conservation of nature: experts recommend eradicating invasive species at once, but only restraining the proliferation of proliferating ones. According to the passage, which question must be asked in order to decide whether to eradicate a rapidly spreading species?
choices: Is it spreading quickly, like an invasive species, or less quickly, like a proliferating one?
Is it a local species, or was it brought from elsewhere?
Has it already established itself, or has it only begun to spread?
Can the size of its population be restrained?
explanation: Origin is the whole distinction; speed, establishment and restrainability are not what separates the two.

steps.stem: The Second World War made cooperation between the British and Belgian governments in the field of diamonds difficult, but did not prevent it. Belgium itself was conquered by Germany, but the Belgian government in exile, which sat in London, did not lose its rule over the Belgian Congo. Thanks to this, the mining of diamonds continued to be managed more or less as usual; but since Antwerp, the diamond capital of the world, was in German hands, the governments of Britain and Belgium were forced to send the diamonds to alternative centers for processing. Which of the following claims does NOT follow from the passage?
choices: The British-Belgian cooperation in diamonds rested on diamonds mined in the Congo
Before the German conquest, Antwerp was a center for the processing of diamonds
The Belgian government sat in London because of its cooperation with Britain in the field of diamonds
The Congo was under Belgian rule before the Second World War
explanation: The government was in London because Belgium was conquered; (1), (2) and (4) each follow.

steps.stem: Although Nietzsche gave the concept "the will to power" a central place in his thought, he never defined precisely what the power the will seeks is. Indeed, the conception of power as the ability to control others and one's surroundings fits many of the occasions on which Nietzsche uses the word — but not all of them. Which of the following claims is made in the passage?
choices: The concept "the will to power" is not central to Nietzsche's thought, and the proof is that he did not define it
Only on a few occasions does Nietzsche use "power" in the sense of control
The conception of power as control is not always the fitting interpretation of the word "power" in Nietzsche's thought
"The will to power" is central to Nietzsche's thought because its meaning is control
explanation: "Many… but not all" is the claim; (2) reverses the proportion, (1) and (4) contradict the passage.

steps.stem: In the United States it was recently enacted that the results of a polygraph test may not be relied upon except for screening candidates for security-sensitive positions. Accordingly, businesses are today forbidden to use a polygraph in screening employees, and forbidden to dismiss an employee because he refused to be tested. Moreover, in the past, when an accused person agreed to a polygraph test, the results were accepted as evidence in the courts of most states, whereas today a polygraph test can no longer serve as evidence in court at all. Which of the following sentences summarizes the passage most precisely?
choices: Apart from exceptional cases, it is forbidden to rely on polygraph results in the United States
In most states it was permitted until recently to compel an employee to take a polygraph test
The American justice system was the first to forbid the use of the polygraph
Today the polygraph is hardly used at all in the American justice system
explanation: (4) softens "not at all" to "hardly"; (2) and (3) are not stated.

steps.stem: In a book on the history of the Lombards it was written: "The Lombards were indeed imbued with a spirit of intolerance, as their sayings testify: 'Whoever is not a Lombard shall have no rights.'" Which of the following claims presents the idea of the sentence most precisely?
choices: The sayings of the Lombards, among them the claim that a non-Lombard has no rights, testify to their great intolerance
The Lombards were not truly intolerant, but their sayings made them appear so
One cannot infer from the sayings of the Lombards that whoever is not a Lombard has no rights
The Lombards said that non-Lombards have no rights only because they were intolerant
explanation: The saying is evidence of the spirit; (4) makes the spirit the cause of the saying, and (2) and (3) deny the passage.

steps.stem: The theater critic Rosicky argued that in his play "Saint Joan," unlike his other plays, George Bernard Shaw created characters who give free expression to their feelings, and that it is therefore easier for the audience to identify with them. Which of the following sentences best expresses Rosicky's claim?
choices: The audience finds it hard to identify with the characters of "Saint Joan" because they express their feelings freely
It is easier for the audience to identify with the characters of "Saint Joan" because, unlike the characters of Shaw's other plays, they give free expression to their feelings
Shaw felt that the characters of "Saint Joan" express their feelings and the feelings of the audience
In all Shaw's plays except "Saint Joan," the characters' expression of strong feelings eases the audience's identification
explanation: (1) reverses the effect; (4) reverses the exception; (3) invents a claim about Shaw.

steps.stem: Professor Lemström held that the rapid growth of plants in the polar regions is caused by the electric currents that flow between the earth and the atmosphere, the currents that also produce the aurora. In his view the pointed needles and fine branches of the fir help to conduct these currents through the plants, and that is the reason for their rapid growth. Which of the following claims is implied by Lemström's words?
choices: The high electrical conductivity of polar plants is a consequence of the aurora
Without the electric currents, polar plants would grow faster
The accelerated growth of polar plants results from electric currents that pass through them thanks to their shape, which makes them better conductors
The aurora is responsible for the accelerated growth of polar plants
explanation: The aurora and the growth are both effects of the currents; (1) and (4) make one effect the cause of the other; (2) reverses the direction.

steps.stem: The English writer J. G. Ballard said: "Even today people like being together — though not in the manner of the old squares of an Italian town of the fifteenth century, for instance, but by standing in a queue for a bus or a lift. This is a new form of togetherness, and at times it may look strange, but it is the distinctive mark of the modern technological age." According to the passage, which of the following claims does Ballard make?
choices: In the past people enjoyed one another's company more than they do today
Before the fifteenth century, crowds in places that were not town squares looked strange
Technology today allows people to gather in places where they could not gather in the past
For people today, standing in a queue for a bus or a lift is a form of being together
explanation: (1) adds a comparison of enjoyment; (2) misplaces "strange"; (3) makes technology a means rather than a mark.

steps.stem: The legal philosopher H. L. A. Hart argues that criminal law contains rules that cannot be explained except as attempts to enforce morality for morality's sake, since they involve nothing that would ordinarily be regarded as harmful to other people. Which of the following claims arises from Hart's words?
choices: Attempts to enforce morality for its own sake are doomed to fail if they are not anchored in criminal law
Criminal law also forbids conduct that does no harm to other people
Harming other people is not necessarily immoral
Rules that eventually cause harm are not required to be part of criminal law
explanation: That is what the rules Hart describes do; (1), (3) and (4) are not his claim.

steps.stem: The psychiatrist Carl Jung noticed more than once, in the course of treatment, that his patients raised ideas and beliefs resembling ideas found in ancient myths, although they had no way of knowing those myths. He concluded from this that there exists a stratum which he called "the collective unconscious," shared by all human beings, from which spring the myths, images and ideas that appear in different cultures around the world and in different periods. How did Jung explain the resemblance between the ideas his patients raised and the ancient myths?
choices: Although the patients did not know the myths, they had been influenced by later stories based on them
The collective unconscious absorbs ideas from various cultures, and therefore even those who never knew them recognize them
The patients had been exposed unconsciously to the ideas in the ancient myths, though one cannot know where
The stratum shared by all human beings, which produced similar myths in different cultures, also produced these ideas in the minds of the patients
explanation: A common source, not transmission: (1), (2) and (3) each keep some route by which the myths reached the patients.

steps.stem: German researchers have developed a new method for mapping the habitats of the various species of mammals in rain forests. Formerly, researchers hid in the forest for this purpose and made observations; in the new method the flies do the work for them. It turns out that carrion flies feed on the flesh of dead animals and retain the DNA of those animals in their bodies. The researchers catch the flies, analyze the DNA in their bodies and so discover what they have eaten; and since carrion flies do not fly far from the carcass, the researchers can know which species live in each area. In the new method, what two things do the researchers do in order to know which species live in each area?
choices: Analysis of the DNA in the bodies of the flies and of the mammals
Recording the place where the flies were caught, and analysis of the DNA in their bodies
Recording the place where the mammals were caught, and analysis of the DNA in their bodies
Observation in the forest, and mapping of the flies' habitats
explanation: The place of capture gives the "where," the DNA gives the "who"; the mammals themselves are never handled.

steps.stem: Questions 134–135 refer to the following news item: "Although the treasury's demand for a reform of the tax policy aroused anger among social organizations, which saw in it harm to the weaker classes, the minister of welfare chose to support it — not because he shrank from a struggle with those classes, or because he shut his eyes to the expected consequences of the reform, but because he knew that if he opposed it he would be unable to spare his ministry's budget a real cut; and so long as his ministry's budget is not cut, he thought, the damage done by the reform will be small." According to the item, which of the following steps is likely to cause the minister of welfare to withdraw his support for the reform?
choices: An announcement by the minister of the treasury that the cut in the welfare budget will be carried out even if the reform is approved
A meeting with the leaders of the weaker classes, at which he will set out the damage the reform will do them
A declaration by the minister of the treasury that the added revenue from the reform will be earmarked for the support of the weaker classes
A conversation with the prime minister, in which the prime minister will stress the importance of helping the weaker classes
explanation: His support rests on sparing his budget; if the cut comes anyway, the reason is gone. (3) would make support easier; (2) and (4) tell him what he already knows.

steps.stem: Which of the following summarizes the news item above most precisely?
choices: The social organizations are angry at the minister of welfare's support for the tax reform, though it is known that he is committed to the weaker classes; his support stems from his belief that otherwise a large cut will be made in his budget

The minister of welfare knew that if he opposed the reform his budget would be cut, and supported it only because he feared the damage of the cut; in response, the social organizations argued that he was ignoring the harm the reform would do to the weak

Unlike the social organizations, which opposed the reform, the minister of welfare understood that it would harm the weak; he agreed to support it only because he thought that supporting it was the only way to prevent a large cut in his budget

The minister of welfare knew that if he opposed the reform his budget would be cut; since he believed that the cut would harm the weak more than the reform would, he supported the reform despite the opposition of the social organizations
explanation: (2) reverses the order of the anger and the support; (3) says the organizations did not understand the harm, which the item contradicts; (1) leaves out the comparison of harms that is the minister's reasoning.

steps.stem: Both the coffee plant and the tea plant contain caffeine, the stimulating substance. As is well known, drinking a cup of coffee has a much stronger stimulating effect than drinking a cup of tea, and so it is easy to suppose that coffee beans contain more caffeine than tea leaves. In fact, a hundred grams of coffee beans contain less caffeine than a hundred grams of tea leaves. Drinking a cup of coffee is more stimulating than drinking a cup of tea not because the concentration of caffeine in coffee beans is higher, but because the quantity of coffee needed to prepare a cup is much larger than the quantity of tea needed for a cup. Which of the following claims arises from the passage?
choices: The stimulating effect of coffee does not stem from the caffeine it contains
Although we think that drinking coffee is more stimulating than drinking tea, in fact drinking tea is more stimulating
The concentration of caffeine in the plant from which a drink is made has no effect on the drink's stimulating power
Had the quantities of tea and of coffee needed for a cup been equal, drinking tea would have been more stimulating than drinking coffee
explanation: Equal quantities would leave the higher concentration of the tea leaves to decide. (1) and (3) deny caffeine any role; (2) contradicts "as is well known."

steps.stem: "Cell ingestion" is the process by which a substance outside a cell is taken into it. There are two kinds: engulfing, in which the cell takes in a foreign body, and drinking, in which the cell takes in liquid from the fluid surrounding it. "Cell expulsion" is the process of expelling surplus substance from the cell: the surplus is packed into small vesicles that are sent to the cell's membrane; the membrane of the vesicle fuses with the membrane of the cell, and the contents of the vesicle are released outside. Which of the following claims is made in the passage?
choices: The membranes of the vesicles used in expulsion become part of the membrane of the cell
When a cell takes in a foreign body, liquid is taken in with it
By drinking, the cell takes back the substances that left it by expulsion
Some cells ingest and others expel
explanation: "Fuses with the membrane of the cell" says so; (2), (3) and (4) are not stated.

steps.stem: The meeting point between the historian and the political sociologist is their shared interest in political events. But unlike the sociologist, who seeks general rules that are not bound to a particular society or period, the historian's first duty is to stress the particular details of each event, and so he tends to emphasize the uniqueness of the subject he studies. Nevertheless, in our day the resemblance between the two grows, and historians can be seen trying to formulate rules shared by the unique events they study. Which of the following is the central claim of the passage regarding historians today?
choices: They engage less than in the past in the study of unique, one-time events
Their task is harder than in the past — to prove to the sociologists the one-time character of events
They emphasize the uniqueness of each event they study less than in the past
Unlike the sociologists, they study more than in the past the resemblance between political events in different societies
explanation: The events are still unique; what changes is the emphasis. (1) changes the objects of study; (4) makes the historians unlike the sociologists in the very respect in which they now resemble them.

steps.stem: In a newspaper article it was written: "All the black prophecies about the expected death of the theater — because of the rise of popular literature, because of the cinema, because of television, because of the sinking of high culture and the public's addiction to more popular forms of entertainment — all of them have failed: the theater flourishes and thrives." Which of the following claims is the central claim of the passage?
choices: Many predicted that the cinema would in the end bring about the decline of the theater, but this prophecy has not come true
Precisely because of the prophecies, the theater became more popular
Unlike the predictions, the theater did not fail to compete with the more popular forms of entertainment
Despite the predictions that the theater would disappear, it enjoys success in our day as well
explanation: (1) takes one cause for the whole; (2) invents a mechanism; (3) narrows the claim to competition.

steps.stem: In his book "Nations before Nationalism," the historian John Armstrong surveys the crystallization of ethnic groups into nations. The book deals with Europe and the Middle East; it begins with the entry of the Indo-European tribes into Europe around the year 2000 BCE, ends at the beginning of the age of nationalism at the start of the eighteenth century, and concentrates on the Middle Ages — the period between the fifth and the fifteenth centuries. According to the passage, in which period does Armstrong place the crystallization of most nations?
choices: The Middle Ages
From the eighteenth century onward
The period before 2000 BCE
At the time of the Indo-European tribes' entry into Europe
explanation: A book on the crystallization of nations concentrates where it thinks it happened; (2) is where the book ends, (3) and (4) where it begins.

steps.stem: Until recently chemists relied on the "Overton rule," according to which the more lipophilic a substance is — that is, the better it dissolves in fats — the more easily it penetrates the membranes of the body's cells. New technological developments made it possible to test the rule: researchers compared four substances and found that there is no direct relation between their lipophilicity and their rate of penetration into cells, and that in fact the reverse of what the rule predicts holds. In their view, if this finding is valid for many other substances as well, it will be possible to develop drugs that penetrate cells much faster than today's. According to the passage, how will drugs that penetrate cells faster be developed?
choices: The new drugs will be based on the substances whose rate of penetration was found to be fastest
